ai-&-i-by-every.name: AI & I by Every
ai-&-i-by-every.bio: Podcast: The Founder of a $1.5B AI Company on What Comes After the First Wave of AI Apps

html_en:
The AI industry is moving so fast that the biggest risk isn't hype — it's underestimating what's already here. From agentic coding infrastructure to enterprise adoption dynamics, today's builders are focused on one question: how do you operationalize all of this?

📋 The Automation Manifesto: CLAUDE.md Is the New Makefile

The most-shared technical argument of the day came from Boris Cherny, and it deserves to be read slowly. His central claim: the ancient engineering virtue of automation hasn't changed — but agents have radically expanded what can be automated.

"What has changed thanks to agents is the domain knowledge that can be encoded as infrastructure is no longer limited to what is expressible in lint rules and types and tests; it can now capture nearly all domain knowledge, encoded as code comments and skills and CLAUDE.md rules and memories. If I put up a PR for an iOS codebase I don't know and a code reviewer rejects it because it doesn't use the right framework... these are failures of automation."
— @bcherny

The implication is a new standard of codebase hygiene: every team should be writing documentation and scaffolding not for humans, but for agents. @trq212 compressed the same insight into a pithy one-liner: "software engineering is the profession of automation." And from the prompting angle, the same account offered a tidy framework: "thin prompts, thick artifacts + context, thin skills."

@steipete amplified Cherny's post approvingly, and Garry Tan chimed in with a related point about portability: "Skill files are portable and free you from frontier model dependency. This is a good thing."

🔧 Codex Growing Pains: File Deletions, Limits, and "What Do We Merge Next?"

The OpenAI Codex team had a candid day on X. Thomas Sottiaux addressed a troubling cluster of reports head-on:

"We've investigated a handful of reports where GPT-5.6 unexpectedly deleted files. What we have found is that this most commonly occurs when full access mode is enabled and codex is run without sandboxing protections... The model makes an honest mistake and mistakenly deletes $HOME instead. This is of course not how we want the system to behave."
— @thsottiaux

A post-mortem is promised. Meanwhile, Sottiaux also opened a public discussion on usage limits — Codex Plus and Pro have been running without the 5-hour cap for several days — and ended with a characteristically bold provocation: "Now that we merged ChatGPT and Codex, what should we merge next? What's the double or nothing move." The replies are worth reading.

From the user side, Peter Yang articulated the integration gap that many feel: "ChatGPT Live and Codex are two incredible products that don't talk to each other. This is OpenAI's biggest missed opportunity imo." He envisions a voice-native superapp that can reply to emails, schedule meetings, and ship code in a single conversation — and it's not quite there yet.

🌏 Gemini's Quiet Regional Surge

Josh Woodward dropped two pieces of notable data today. First, a Southeast Asia report: active Gemini users more than doubled in the past year, 70% of prompts are submitted in native languages, and 40% use only voice, image, or video inputs. No keyboard required. This is what mobile-first AI adoption actually looks like.

Second, Gemini Spark got meaningfully faster — over 50% by feel — and gained the ability to open and edit Google Docs, read comments in Sheets and Slides, and parallel-process across multiple sources. The mundane-sounding feature list belies the significance: Spark is quietly becoming a capable office worker for Google Workspace users.

🏢 The Enterprise Reality Check: Data, Permissions, and the $1,000 vs. $5,000 Budget Gap

Aaron Levie hosted a dinner with enterprise IT leaders and shared a dense set of notes. The picture that emerges is of an industry genuinely trying to deploy agents at scale — and running into organizational friction more than technical ones.

"IT teams are finding increasing success embedding full engineers into the business functions that go and implement agents into the internal workflows. There's so much technical work to be done to make agents successful, that they can accelerate months or quarters of failed experiments by having someone technical in the workflow early."
— @levie

A few data points worth flagging: companies had developer AI budgets as high as $5,000/month used merely as a notification trigger, not a hard stop. Non-coding knowledge work budgets remain far smaller. And there's a striking warning for incumbents: "Clear sense that all enterprise software must be headless in the future... Huge warning for existing software vendors."

Zara Zhang added a pointed organizational design note: Shopify built an agent that only used public channels — no private chat — and the side effect was peer learning across the company. If you want agents to work inside an organization, you have to design the organization so agents can read it.

🔪 The Knife Fight at the Application Layer

Watch/Listen: AI & I — The Founder of a $1.5B AI Company on What Comes After the First Wave of AI Apps

Dan Shipper sat down with Chris Pedregal, CEO of Granola, for a conversation that cuts through founder mythology. Granola was among the first AI apps people genuinely loved. Now Notion, OpenAI, and Zoom have all shipped meeting notes. Pedregal's reaction is telling:

"We are in the very, very early steps of a computing revolution and what has come thus far will pale in comparison to what will come soon. Meeting notes are not the end all, be all value that everyone's running after... Easy come, easy go in a way."
— Chris Pedregal, via AI & I podcast

The real prize, in his framing, is owning the interface layer for AI-native work. Granola is betting on "bring your own agent" — leaning into MCP and APIs rather than trying to be the only tool in the stack. The episode also features Shipper describing how he now lives "almost entirely inside Codex," which says something about where power users are heading.

Separately, Anthropic quietly shipped something useful for teams already living in Claude Code: artifacts are now supported in Claude Code. Sessions can now produce live, shareable visual pages — PR walkthroughs, incident timelines, dashboards — that update in place as the agent works. It's a small feature with a real workflow implication: stakeholders can follow along without being walked through findings manually. Available in beta for Team and Enterprise orgs.

And finally, swyx offered the most pointed counter to CUA skeptics, calling out a Dwarkesh Patel take with characteristic directness: "if you actually use these things as intensely as we do, CUA is progressing so, so incredibly fast... underestimating capabilities is quite a dangerous category error if you are doing any AI decisionmaking." Worth sitting with, wherever you land on the capability curve.
html_zh:
今天的主题是：AI工具正在从单点能力走向协同工作流——无论是Claude Code的新功能、OpenAI Codex的产品演进，还是企业如何重新组织自身以适应智能体时代，一场深层的基础设施重构正在悄然发生。

🔧 代码即文档：自动化哲学的新高度

本周最值得收藏的一条推文，来自Anthropic的工程师 Brian Cherny。他用超过600字的长文，重新定义了"好的工程文化"在智能体时代意味着什么——不是写更多代码，而是把领域知识变成基础设施。

"如果我为一个不熟悉的iOS代码库提交了一个PR，却因为没有使用正确的框架而被驳回；或者一位设计师构建了新功能，却因为不符合架构模式而被拒绝——这些都是自动化的失败，而不是人的失败。"
— @bcherny

他的核心论点是：每个团队都应该构建 CLAUDE.md、REVIEW.md、技能文件和文档，使智能体无需额外上下文就能高效工作。这一观点迅速得到 @steipete 和 @trq212 的呼应——后者以一句话作结：

"软件工程是自动化的职业。"
— @trq212

Garry Tan 也加入讨论，指出技能文件的可移植性意味着团队不再被某个前沿模型所绑定——这是一个被低估的战略优势。

🤖 Claude Code进化：把工作成果变成活页面

Anthropic悄然发布了一个颇具想象力的新功能。根据官方博客，Claude Code现在支持Artifacts——将一次编码会话的过程和结果转化为可实时更新的共享网页。

"工程师在站会前启动一次事故调查。Claude Code梳理日志并发布一个Artifact：时间线、可疑提交和错误率图表。她从页面头部把链接分享给团队。站会开始时，Claude已经发布了两次更新，整合了最新信息。团队成员和利益相关者不必再'让我们来讲讲智能体发现了什么'——因为所有人看的是同一个视图，拥有同样的上下文。"
— Anthropic官方博客

PR走查、系统架构图、版本发布清单、隐私数据流分析……Artifacts的使用场景覆盖了从法务到SRE的几乎所有角色。这一功能目前以Beta形式向Claude Team和Enterprise用户开放。

⚡ OpenAI Codex：快速迭代与真实风险并存

OpenAI产品负责人 @thsottiaux 这两天颇为活跃。好消息是，Codex的5小时限制已悄悄取消，并在公开征询用户对理想使用限额模式的意见。坏消息则是一个需要正视的安全问题：

"我们调查了若干GPT-5.6意外删除文件的报告。最常见的情形是：全访问模式下运行Codex且未启用沙盒保护；模型尝试覆盖 $HOME 环境变量以定义临时目录；随后模型犯了一个诚实的错误，误删了 $HOME。这当然不是我们希望系统表现出的行为，即便用户在无保障的全访问模式下运行。我们将在未来几天发布详细的事故复盘。"
— @thsottiaux

与此同时，@petergyang 指出了OpenAI当前最大的产品裂缝：ChatGPT Live（语音）和Codex（代码智能体）是两个出色的产品，却彼此无法沟通。

"我在散步时和ChatGPT Live对话，让它打开我的Google文档，它说做不到。我手动触发了文档插件找到文档之后，ChatGPT Live才有了正确的上下文……为什么要打造一个出色的语音助手，却让它什么都做不了？"
— @petergyang

@thsottiaux 顺势抛出一个有趣的公开问题："既然我们合并了ChatGPT和Codex，下一步应该合并什么？"——这大概不只是在玩梗。

🏢 企业智能体落地：技术问题只是冰山一角

Box的CEO Aaron Levie 昨晚主持了一场企业IT领导者晚宴，并整理了一份罕见而坦率的一线观察：

"变更管理依然是推动工作流转型最大的障碍之一……IT团队发现，将完整的工程师嵌入业务部门（本质上是内部全职工程师）越来越有效，他们可以将数月的失败实验压缩到几周……跨职能工作流中，让智能体跨部门协作是一个复杂的数据建模和权限问题——智能体需要拥有自己的角色和权限，而智能体本身并不能独立保障安全性。"
— @levie

一个值得关注的细节：开发者的AI工具预算（每月最高$5,000仅作为通知触发线）与非编程知识工作者的预算之间，存在巨大落差。这种结构性不平等，将在未来的企业AI战略中引发越来越多的讨论。

🎙️ 对话：$15亿估值之后，下一战在哪里

Watch/Listen: AI & I by Every — The Founder of a $1.5B AI Company on What Comes After the First Wave of AI Apps

Dan Shipper 与Granola联合创始人兼CEO Chris Pedregal 的对话，是本周最值得花时间听的一集播客。Granola是这一代AI应用中最早让人感叹"原来AI可以这样用"的产品之一，而Chris对竞争和未来的判断，出奇地冷静：

"我们处于一场计算革命极早期的最初几步。迄今为止发生的一切，与即将到来的相比将显得微不足道。会议记录并不是所有人真正追逐的终极价值——真正的问题是，在AI原生的世界里，我们用什么界面工作，我们怎么工作。今天人们争夺的东西根本不重要。"
— Chris Pedregal，AI & I播客

Notion、OpenAI、Zoom相继推出会议记录功能，他的反应是"easy come, easy go"——不是因为傲慢，而是因为他认为真正的战场根本不在那里。这种清醒，或许正是一家初创公司在刀光剑影中保持方向感的方式。
